name: David Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello David, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a buyer at Harlow and Dunn, a plumbing and heating supplier. I get in at 7:30, check overnight stock levels on the system, then spend the morning phoning reps about boilers, copper pipe and valves. Afternoons are price negotiations and chasing late deliveries. By five my ears hurt from the phone, but I like that I know the reps by name.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like landing a good deal, like getting a rep to hold last year's price on fittings for another quarter. What wears me out is the pressure to hit margin targets that go up every year while my pay doesn't. I'm 43, with Nadia, two kids and a mortgage, so I can't afford to rock the boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, then, because most of the hype never came with anything real. At work I'd tell the lads the stock-checking software saves a few minutes and that's about it. Online I'd keep quiet. I don't post about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, between us, it means I keep my job for now but nothing gets easier. The mortgage is the same, the margin targets keep going up, and the company still squeezes us. I've been at Harlow and Dunn 14 years and I still feel one bad quarter from a restructure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd keep phoning my reps, because a call gets you a better price than an email. I'd also put another 100 a month into the savings account, which has about three months of bills in it. That's all the room I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, but not relaxed. The plateau means no robots at my desk, which is a relief. It doesn't fix the fact that money's tight and the kids' school trips cost more every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use any AI tools yourself. Is that a choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've never touched those tools, no. I like doing things the way I know, and I don't trust a program with a 40,000 order. If it gets one price wrong, it's my name on it, not the program's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill gets squeezed first if the company has a bad year anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday goes first, then eating out, then I'd stop topping up the kids' savings. The mortgage never gets touched. Nadia and I talked about it last winter when the boiler broke and we paid 900 for the repair.

say: AI is **mostly hype**, and I'd tell colleagues it saves a few minutes at best.
I'd stay **quiet** online, because I don't post about work.
think: My job is **safe for now**, but I still feel one bad quarter from a restructure.
The **mortgage** and the rising margin targets are the pressure, not AI.
do: Keep phoning reps because a call gets a **better price** than email.
Put another **100 a month** into savings, which holds about three months of bills.
feel: **Steady** but not relaxed, since money stays tight either way.
S0.quote: The mortgage is the same, the margin targets keep going up, and the company still squeezes us.
fieldNote: David sounds calm but his worry is **money** and targets, not AI.
He trusts **phone** relationships over software and says he never uses AI tools.

steps.text: Keep phoning reps on the main boiler and pipe accounts
Add 100 a month to the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the companies that decide, not the software. If they use AI to cut buyers, that's a choice by the bosses. At work I'd say we need a proper agreement on how any of it gets introduced, and I'd raise it at the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it scares me. Reordering, checking stock and comparing supplier prices are exactly the parts a program can do. What's left is the phone calls, and I can't tell if that's enough to keep a whole team of six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union rep first and ask what the company has promised. I'd also ask my manager Priya which of my tasks are staying with me. And I'd quietly start looking at the other distributors in town, because there are a few, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knotted stomach. I keep thinking about Nadia's face if I came home and said they'd cut two buyers. We'd get through three months, maybe four, and then it gets hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks would the software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The reorder lists, no question. I spend about two hours a day on those. If the software does that and keeps the stock right, they will ask why they need six of us when four can handle the calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if your team shrank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd blame the shareholders and the executives who treat people as a cost line. I'd also be angry that nobody in government makes them show what they plan to do with the jobs. There should be rules on that, with some warning for workers.

say: It's the **bosses** who decide, not the software, and we need a proper **agreement** on it.
I'd raise it at the **union** meeting before anything gets introduced.
think: Reordering and price checks are the parts a program can do, and that leaves **fewer buyers**.
I can't tell if **phone calls** alone justify a team of six.
do: Ask my manager Priya which tasks **stay with me**, and ask the union rep what's promised.
Quietly look at the other **distributors** in town, just in case.
feel: **Knotted stomach**, thinking about telling Nadia two buyers were cut.
S1.quote: Reordering, checking stock and comparing supplier prices are exactly the parts a program can do.
fieldNote: His fear is specific: the **reorder lists** take two hours a day and are the easiest to automate.
He frames it as a bosses' choice and turns first to the **union**, not to learning new tools.

steps.text: Ask manager Priya which tasks stay on my desk
Raise the rollout plan at the next union meeting
Look at job ads from three other distributors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not acceptable that something this big can land in two years with no plan. At work I'd push the union to demand notice, retraining and pay protection. Online I'd probably share anything about a government response, because someone has to answer for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished in this job. Buying is thinking work, which is exactly what arrives first, and two years is nothing. With three months saved and a mortgage, I'd have until about spring before it gets frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd cut every extra: the streaming, the gym, the weekend trips. I'd go to the bank about the mortgage before I'm behind. I'd ask Nadia to take extra shifts at the clinic. And I'd push the union hard, because alone I've got nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor going. I've never been a risk taker, and now the choices are all risky. I'd probably lie awake doing sums on the back of an envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Nadia that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her straight: Nadia, it might be the end of my job and we need to protect the house. She'd be scared but she'd stay steady. Then we'd sit the kids down more gently and say we're being careful with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it matter to you that robots come three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters a bit. Hands-on work gets three more years, so the warehouse lads and the delivery drivers last longer than I do. That's a strange thing, being the one with the degree and the first to go. But I couldn't retrain as a plumber at 43 with two kids.

say: It's **not acceptable** that this lands in two years with no plan.
I'd push the **union** to demand notice, retraining and pay protection.
think: I think my **job is finished**, because buying is thinking work and it goes first.
With three months saved, it gets **frightening** by spring.
do: Cut the **streaming**, the gym and weekend trips, and talk to the bank about the mortgage.
Ask Nadia to take **extra shifts** while I push the union.
feel: Like the **floor going**, with only risky choices left.
S2.quote: Buying is thinking work, which is exactly what arrives first, and two years is nothing.
fieldNote: David expects his own job to go and says so plainly, so this is **alarmed**, not just anxious.
He stays **disciplined**: cuts spending, calls the bank early and leans on the union.

steps.text: Cancel streaming and the gym and drop weekend trips
Call the bank about mortgage options before missing payments
Press the union to demand notice and retraining
Ask Nadia to take extra clinic shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to plan if people are honest about it. At work I'd tell the younger buyers to get a second skill now. I'd also say the government needs to set up retraining that people can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years gives me a chance but not a guarantee. I'm 48 by then, with the kids teenagers. If my job goes in 2031, I need to be earning from something else, and I don't know yet what that is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to pay down the mortgage as fast as I can, cutting the car to one. Then I'd find a night course in logistics or supply planning, something that touches real warehouses. And I'd join the union steering group so I'm not alone when it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than two years, but there's a lump in my throat. Time feels like a gift and a deadline at once. I know myself, I'd put it off and then panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra three years compared to two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm scrambling. Five years, I can do a course, clear a chunk of the mortgage, and look around. But if I just wait, it's the same trap as the short one with a little more notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, my manager, because she's two years from needing a different job and she has a daughter at university. And Tomasz on the buying team, who's 29 and just got his first flat. They don't talk about it, but I see it in how they look at the new software demos.

say: Five years is **long enough** to plan if people are honest about it.
I'd tell younger buyers to get a **second skill** now.
think: Five years gives me a **chance**, but not a guarantee.
If I only wait, it's the **same trap** as the short one with a little more notice.
do: Pay down the **mortgage** faster and cut the family to one car.
Start a night course in **logistics** and join the union steering group.
feel: **Relief** and a deadline at once, with a lump in my throat.
S3.quote: Five years gives me a chance but not a guarantee. I'm 48 by then, with the kids teenagers.
fieldNote: David says time helps only if he acts, and he admits he tends to **put things off**.
Extra years move him from alarmed to anxious because he sees a **plan** he could follow.

steps.text: Pay down the mortgage faster and run one car
Enrol in a night course in logistics planning
Join the union steering group at Harlow and Dunn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and we should use it to build a fair system, with retraining funded and rules for companies. At work I'd say don't panic yet, but don't ignore it. And I'd keep saying the unions need to be at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years takes the edge off my own situation. I'd be 53, the kids grown or nearly, the mortgage close to paid. The job might go but it wouldn't catch me at my most exposed. The real worry is the pay gap, with a few people owning all the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job well and pay the mortgage down faster. I'd learn some basic AI tools, finally, because if I'm going to sit in a union meeting arguing about it, I should know what I'm arguing about. And I'd push Zain and Layla toward careers with people in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. I'd still read the news and get a bad feeling, but day to day I'd sleep fine. A decade is time to adjust, and my kids would be the ones who really face it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change what you tell your kids about careers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to pick work that involves caring for people or hands-on skills. A trade or nursing, like their mum. I'd tell them degrees in desk work are not the safe bet they used to be, and I know that's rich coming from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you feel safe in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper income guarantee, for one. And a law that says companies must give two years' notice before swapping staff for AI. If that was in place, I'd stop being so afraid and just get on with my life.

say: Ten years is a **long runway**, and unions need to be at the table.
I'd tell colleagues **don't panic**, but don't ignore it.
think: Ten years takes the edge off, since I'd be **53** with the mortgage nearly paid.
My real worry is **inequality**, with a few people owning all the machines.
do: Pay the **mortgage** down faster and learn some basic AI tools.
Steer **Zain and Layla** toward caring or hands-on careers.
feel: **Calmer** day to day, with the kids the ones who really face it.
S4.quote: I'd tell my kids to pick work that involves caring for people or hands-on skills.
fieldNote: David is the least afraid here because the **mortgage** would be nearly paid by then.
He finally accepts he should try AI tools, mainly so he can argue from **knowledge**.

steps.text: Pay the mortgage down faster each year
Try a basic AI tool for a month on reorder lists
Push for a two-year notice law through the union
Steer Zain and Layla toward trades or nursing

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, without a doubt. Two years with three months of savings isn't enough for anyone. What would help is notice, a proper retraining budget and the union at the table with the company. A fair deal on the mortgage side would help too, because the house is what we can't lose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not against the technology. I'm against it being done to us rather than with us. I keep thinking that Nadia and the kids shouldn't pay for a decision someone made in a boardroom.

headlineQuote: I'm not against the technology. I'm against it being done to us rather than with us.
portrait: David is a **43-year-old** buyer at a plumbing supplier, with a partner, two children and a mortgage.
He trusts **phone calls** and the union over software, and has never used AI tools.
His fear is specific: the **reorder lists** and price checks could go first, leaving too few buyers.
He copes by **cutting spending**, calling the bank early and pushing for collective rules.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most, because two years with three months saved isn't enough.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice**, funded retraining and the union at the table, plus mortgage help.
